## Outside checks

HISTOR is not the only public record of MCP tool definitions. Where another log publishes its reads, the two are compared on the same servers and days, and the result is published both ways, with HISTOR's own misses.

### ScraperWatch

A daily diff of a fixed panel of about 3,000 remote endpoints. HISTOR compares each of their published days with its own reads, and ScraperWatch shows the result on its page under "Outside check". The first comparison found a robots.txt parsing limit on their side and a handshake regression on HISTOR's; both were fixed the same day.

### heldfast

An open daily record of the tool definitions of the servers in the official MCP registry. Of the 23,190 servers both logs recorded on 26 October 2026, 21,215 had every field in both; on those, 97.9% of servers and 99.1% of tools were identical byte for byte, and each difference has a stated cause: package versions, read times, failed reads, a first page only, an older protocol.

## Use it

Before your agent trusts a server, send the tools it received. The answer is signed by the log's did:key and names the tree head it was given under.
    
    curl -sS https://histor.modelmarket.dev/api/v1/check \
      -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
      -d '{"endpoint":"https://example.com/mcp","tools":[ …tools/list result… ],"contribute":true}'
    # -> {"type":"histor.check/v1","match":"same"|"different"|"previously-observed"|…,
    #     "observed":{"unchangedSince":"…","changes":0}, "patternScan":{…}, "signature":{…}}
    
    # README badge for your server
    [![MCP tool defs](https://histor.modelmarket.dev/badge/<id>.svg)](https://histor.modelmarket.dev/s/<id>)
    
    # Atom feed of every observed change

## Questions

Is this a marketplace listing?

No. The server list is the log's index: every remote endpoint in the official MCP registry, with what HISTOR could observe about it. Nothing here is for sale and nothing is ranked by quality.

Does HISTOR tell me a server is safe?

No, and it never will. It tells you what a server advertised, whether that changed, and which published patterns matched the text. Whether to trust the server is your decision — HISTOR makes sure you decide on the same facts as everyone else.

Why are so many servers "not observed"?

Most remote MCP endpoints require a login (they answer 401 to anyone without a key), some use the legacy SSE transport or need per-user values in the URL, and some are simply down. They stay on the list with the reason, so the numbers never hide them.

How do I check a server I already use?

Open the Check tab, paste the server's endpoint and the tools/list result your client received, and press Check. --------------------------------------------------------------------------------

An npm or PyPI server is observed under the test conditions above: Linux, no internet, placeholder keys. One that needs Windows, a real account or the network may show fewer tools or none; its page says why it exited.

### One operator, one key

Today one party runs the log. A second observer on another network is the next step, and any AIMarket hub can run one. Until then, what the key proves is who said it — not that it is true.

### Behind a login, unseen

Endpoints that require authentication answer 401 to everyone without a key, including HISTOR. They are counted and listed as not observed, never dropped from the numbers.

## Questions

Is this a marketplace listing?

No. The server list is the log's index: every remote endpoint in the official MCP registry, with what HISTOR could observe about it. Nothing here is for sale and nothing is ranked by quality.

Does HISTOR tell me a server is safe?

No, and it never will. It tells you what a server advertised, whether that changed, and which published patterns matched the text. Whether to trust the server is your decision — HISTOR makes sure you decide on the same facts as everyone else.

Why are so many servers "not observed"?

Most remote MCP endpoints require a login (they answer 401 to anyone without a key), some use the legacy SSE transport or need per-user values in the URL, and some are simply down. They stay on the list with the reason, so the numbers never hide them.

How do I check a server I already use?

Open the Check tab, paste the server's endpoint and the tools/list result your client received, and press Check. You get back, signed, whether HISTOR observed the same definitions — or different ones, or an older set.

How do I get a badge for my server?

Find your endpoint on the Servers tab, open it, and copy the Markdown snippet under the facts. The badge shows the date your definitions were pinned or last changed, and links to the full history.

Why should I trust HISTOR itself?

You do not have to. Every label and every tree head is signed with one published key; the Log tab proves in your browser that the log only grew; and the command-line auditor does the same from any machine. What remains is that one operator runs it today — a second, independent observer is the next step.

What does it cost?

Looking things up, the badges, the feed and /check are free. HISTOR also offers histor.check@v1 to the AIMarket Hub, so agents can reach it through the market.

I run an MCP server. What does HISTOR send it, and how do I opt out?

Every 6 hours, and every 30 minutes for a week once its tools have changed twice in a week. First it reads /robots.txt (RFC 9309, product token histor, about once a day per site): a path that file does not allow HISTOR is not read, and its page here says so. --------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## What this means for MCP crawlers

Most of those Disallow lines were written for search engines: `/api/`, `/dashboard`, `/admin`. Whether a monitor or an MCP client should honour them for an endpoint the publisher has listed in the MCP registry is a fair question. ScraperWatch honours robots.txt. Until 2 November HISTOR didn't consult it for registry-listed servers; since then it does, reading the `histor` group, or `*` if there is none, with RFC 9309's longest match. On the registry snapshot of 26 October, 4,708 of 33,520 remote endpoints (14%) disallow it. HISTOR's page for each of them says so and names the rule. Where robots.txt allows it, HISTOR still reads the server's MCP server card, the operator's own list of its tools.

If your crawler does honour robots.txt, it should read the file the way the site meant it. Concretely:

  * Run Python 3.13.14+, 3.14.5+ or 3.15. On 3.12 or older, use a parser that implements RFC 9309 rather than `urllib.robotparser`.
  * Test with `Allow: /` first and with a `$` rule. The four lines above cover the first; `Allow: /api/mcp$` before `Disallow: /api/` covers the second.
  * If you publish an MCP endpoint and want agents to reach it, `Allow: /api/mcp$` is correct, and the longest-match rule makes it work in any order. Crawlers on old Python will still miss it. A plain `Allow: /api/mcp` without the `$`, placed before the Disallow, works in both, at the cost of also allowing everything below that path.

Limits: one fetch per host from one network on one day, and only the `*` group. A crawler with a named group in a file can get a different answer.

# We read the robots.txt of 2,347 MCP hosts: Python 3.12's parser gets 252 endpoints wrong

#python#webdev#mcp#opensource

Two crawlers that log MCP servers compared notes on 1 November, and one server didn't add up. www.apier.no had changed its tool definitions twice in a day. Our log, HISTOR, recorded both changes. ScraperWatch, which honours robots.txt, skipped the server entirely. Its robots.txt looked clear enough (an excerpt; the group has twelve more Allow lines):
    
    `User-agent: *
    Allow: /api/mcp$
    Disallow: /api/
    `

The site even explains the order in a comment: Allow lines come first so that first-match crawlers let the public paths through. ScraperWatch's crawler used Python's `urllib.robotparser`, and it still said no. ScraperWatch switched to an RFC 9309 reader the same day.

We wanted to know whether that was one unlucky server or a pattern. So we fetched the robots.txt of every host on ScraperWatch's panel, 2,347 hosts behind 2,995 MCP endpoints drawn at random from the official MCP registry. ## The survey

On 1 November between 19:06 and 19:10 UTC we made one request to `https://<host>/robots.txt` for each of the 2,347 hosts. We followed redirects and stopped at 10 seconds. Then we ran the same script under two interpreters. Each asked `urllib.robotparser` whether a crawler with no group of its own, so the `*` group applies, may fetch each endpoint:

 | 
--- | ---
hosts  | 2,347
a real robots.txt with at least one group  | 1,315
an HTML page or no groups  | 261
404  | 514
no answer, other 4xx, 5xx  | 257
MCP endpoints on hosts with a robots.txt  | 1,764
disallowed by Python 3.14.8 (RFC 9309)  | 421
disallowed by Python 3.12.13 (first match)  | 173
endpoints where the two disagree  | 252 (14.3%)

As a third opinion we ran HISTOR's own RFC 9309 reader, written separately for our cross-checks. It agrees with Python 3.14.8 on all 1,764.

The disagreement runs almost entirely one way. On 250 endpoints, the old parser says "go ahead" where the site said no. On 2 it says no where the site said yes.

ScraperWatch found the same in its own log. ## `$` written for agents

The other 34 involve `*` or `$`. The two endpoints that the old parser wrongly refuses are the most interesting, because both sites wrote their rules for AI agents on purpose:

  * www.apier.no: `Allow: /api/mcp$` before `Disallow: /api/`.
  * api.adplug.app: nine lines like `Allow: /mcp/linkedin-ads$`, one per MCP endpoint, then `Disallow: /mcp`.

Both open exactly the MCP endpoint and nothing under it. To the old parser, `/api/mcp$` is a literal path with a dollar sign at the end, which no URL has, so the Allow never matches and the broad Disallow wins. The sites that tried hardest to welcome agents are the ones a Python 3.12 crawler turns away.

## What this means for MCP crawlers

Most of those Disallow lines were written for search engines: `/api/`, `/dashboard`, `/admin`. Whether a monitor or an MCP client should honour them for an endpoint the publisher has listed in the MCP registry is a fair question. ScraperWatch honours robots.txt. Until 2 November HISTOR didn't consult it for registry-listed servers; since then it does, reading the `histor` group, or `*` if there is none, with RFC 9309's longest match. On the registry snapshot of 26 October, 4,708 of 33,520 remote endpoints (14%) disallow it. HISTOR's page for each of them says so and names the rule. Where robots.txt allows it, HISTOR still reads the server's MCP server card, the operator's own list of its tools.

If your crawler does honour robots.txt, it should read the file the way the site meant it. Concretely:

  * Run Python 3.13.14+, 3.14.5+ or 3.15. On 3.12 or older, use a parser that implements RFC 9309 rather than `urllib.robotparser`.
  * Test with `Allow: /` first and with a `$` rule. The four lines above cover the first; `Allow: /api/mcp$` before `Disallow: /api/` covers the second.
  * If you publish an MCP endpoint and want agents to reach it, `Allow: /api/mcp$` is correct, and the longest-match rule makes it work in any order. Crawlers on old Python will still miss it. A plain `Allow: /api/mcp` without the `$`, placed before the Disallow, works in both, at the cost of also allowing everything below that path.

## Data

Everything is at https://histor.modelmarket.dev/datasets/robots-mcp-hosts-2026-11-01/: - the panel; - the fetch script and the 2,347 responses; - the script that runs under each interpreter; - the 252 disagreements with the rules that caused them.

The panel itself is ScraperWatch's: https://scraperwatch.com/mcp-changes/panel.txt.

Limits: one fetch per host from one network on one day, and only the `*` group. A crawler with a named group in a file can get a different answer.
